text: The bell for lunch break rings at Meridian Public School, and within a minute the corridor smells of six different homes. Aarav opens his tiffin — lemon rice, still warm. Ira opens hers — two rotis and a bowl of dal. From the next bench comes the smell of fish curry, from the bench behind, of dhokla.
Aarav looks around the room: the lunches differ. Which ingredients do they share, and what does the body obtain from them?
So what is actually happening inside all those tiffin boxes? Why does food make us able to run, and think, and grow?
Look at your own lunch today. Name three things in it. Where did each one come from?
3.1 What Do We Eat in a Week?
Aarav's question is a good one, and the honest answer is that we cannot say much about food in general until we look at food in particular. So begin with the food you know best: your own.

Most of us eat without paying attention. We eat what is served, at the time it is served, and we rarely notice the pattern. But there is pattern. Over a week, your meals repeat, vary, and cluster in ways that tell you something about your household, your region, and your health.

Scientists call this kind of careful watching observation. Observation is not the same as looking. Looking is what you do all day. Observing is looking with a question in mind, and writing down what you find.
Activity 3.1 — Keep a food diary
In your notebook, use two columns: Day and What I ate and drank. Record one entry for each day, Monday to Sunday.
Now read your table as a scientist would. Did the same items appear on most days? Which days were different from the rest, and can you say why — a festival, a guest, a day you were unwell?

Next, compare. Ask three classmates to show you their tables. Find one food that appears in all four diaries, and one food that appears in only one. Comparing is how we tell what is common from what is particular.
Your diaries may share ingredients, but check rather than assume this. A food absent from four diaries may appear in another household. Four diaries cannot represent the whole class or region.
So even inside a single classroom, food is not one thing. It varies. The next question is why.
3.1.1 Food varies from place to place
A traveller eating in Amritsar, Bengaluru and Imphal could find different dishes and shared ingredients. A regional label does not describe every household. Compare examples before generalising.
That is not an accident, and it is not only a matter of taste. Let us gather the evidence first and explain it afterwards.
Activity 3.2 — Map the food of India
Table 3.2 — Crops and food across Indian states
Now analyse your completed table. Read down the "crops" column and then down the "dishes" column, and look for a relationship between the two.
The examples link wheat with Punjabi dishes, ragi with dishes in Karnataka, and rice with dishes in Manipur. Is the same relationship present in your other rows? Look for an exception as well.
Local crops can influence food traditions, but proximity alone does not guarantee the cheapest or freshest food. Transport, storage, season and farming costs also matter.

Soil, rainfall and temperature affect which crops grow well. Rice is often grown in flooded fields, though not all rice requires standing water. Ragi can tolerate relatively dry conditions. Farmers can also change irrigation and soil management.

Soil and climate are not the whole story. Culture, religion and history all shape what a community eats and what it avoids. Two families in the same street, growing food from the same fields, may cook very differently.
Regional food reflects crops, trade, cost, taste, culture and tradition. A crops-and-dishes table suggests relationships; it does not isolate a single cause.
Choose a dish common in your state. Is it also eaten across the border? Check with two sources before explaining any difference using crops, trade or tradition.
3.1.2 Food also varies from time to time

Food varies across the map. Does it also vary across the years? Interview an older person about dishes, fuel and cooking tools. Record continuity as well as change; one memory cannot represent every household.
Activity 3.3 — Interview an elder
Cooking tools, then and now
Fig. 3.1 · (a) Chulha — traditional wood-fired stove (b) Modern gas stove
(c) Sil-batta — stone grinder (d) Electric mixer-grinder
Pool the class's interview notes and a shared picture appears. The way food is prepared — what we can call culinary practice — has changed sharply within living memory.

A chulha burns fuel such as wood or dung cakes; a gas stove burns gas. A sil-batta grinds food by hand; a mixer-grinder uses an electric motor. These tools coexist today. Your interviews can show which changes occurred in particular homes and when.
Why did all this change?
Partly because the technology arrived. Gas connections, electricity and affordable appliances reached ordinary households, and once a tool that saves an hour a day is available, people use it.

Partly because transport improved. Roads, railways and cold storage mean that a fruit grown in Himachal can be sold in Chennai. Foods that were once purely local became available everywhere, and cuisines began to borrow from each other.
Television, phones and the internet can spread recipes beyond a region. To test a claim about how quickly one dish spread, we would need dated evidence from several places.

Change of this kind brings real gains. Cooking takes less time — which matters most to the women who have historically done most of it. Fuel-efficient stoves mean less smoke indoors, and less smoke means healthier lungs.

Changes can also reduce the use of familiar grains or cooking skills. Whether a replacement is more nourishing depends on its ingredients, preparation and quantity. Compare examples rather than assuming that older or newer food is better.

Smoke in the kitchen A wood or dung chulha burning indoors fills a kitchen with fine smoke. Breathing that smoke for years damages the lungs and the heart, and the person standing closest to the stove breathes the most of it. This is one reason governments have worked to bring clean cooking fuel to rural households: a better stove is a health measure, not just a convenience.
3.2 What Is Food Made Of?
Aarav misses breakfast and feels hungry during class. Ira shares a banana at break. Later he says he feels better.
Does that observation prove what caused the change? Rest, water and other factors may matter too. We need knowledge of digestion to explain what food can supply; this story is not a blood-sugar test.

Something in food, then, is not the same as food. When we eat a banana we are not eating "banana" as far as the body is concerned. We are eating a mixture of substances, each of which the body uses for a different job. These substances are the components of food.
Different foods carry different components in different amounts. That is why no single food keeps a person well, and why the mixture on the plate matters as much as the items on it.
Begin with carbohydrates, one group of food components.
Carbohydrates

Glucose is a simple sugar and a carbohydrate. Cells can release energy from glucose. Starch is also a carbohydrate; digestion breaks it down into smaller sugars before absorption. Foods supply mixtures, so a banana is not a dose of pure glucose.

We rarely eat pure glucose. We eat carbohydrates in the form of cereals — wheat, rice, maize, jowar; in root vegetables — potato and sweet potato; and in fruits — banana, mango, pineapple, sugarcane. Ordinary table sugar is a carbohydrate too.
Fig. 3.2 · Some sources of carbohydrates
Fats

Ghee and cooking oils contain fats. Fat supplies about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrate. The body can use fat for energy or store it; it does not automatically store all dietary fat. Stored fat also cushions organs and reduces heat loss. These functions do not establish a special need for laddoos in winter.

Fats come from plants and from animals. Plant sources include groundnut, walnut, cashew, almond, pistachio, coconut, sesame seed, pumpkin seed, sunflower seed, soya bean and the oils pressed from them. Animal sources include butter, ghee, curd and milk.
Fig. 3.3 · Some sources of fats

Stored fat in a polar bear: pregnant females can spend months in a den without feeding, drawing on stored reserves while giving birth and nursing cubs. Most other polar bears remain active and hunt through winter. Fat also provides insulation.
Name three foods you ate this week that contained a visible fat. Where did each fat come from — a plant or an animal?
Proteins

Carbohydrates and fats supply energy, and fats also form parts of cells. Proteins have an essential role in building and repairing tissues. These job labels overlap; they are not exclusive compartments.

Consider what a body has to do besides move. A six-year-old grows into a sixteen-year-old. A cut on your hand closes over in a week. Hair grows, nails grow, muscle thickens with training. All of that is construction work, and construction needs material.
The material is protein.

Proteins are used to build new tissue and repair damaged tissue. This is why the diet of a growing child must contain enough protein, and why an athlete training for strength needs more than a person who is not. A body short of protein cannot grow properly, however much energy it is given — you cannot build a wall out of firewood.

Pulses, soya beans, nuts and seeds supply protein. Milk, curd, paneer, eggs, fish and meat are other sources. Compare amounts as well as presence: fresh mushrooms contain protein but are mostly water and supply less per usual serving than pulses.
Because of the job they do, protein-rich foods are called body-building foods — while carbohydrates and fats, which supply energy, are together called energy-giving foods.
Fig. 3.4 · Plant sources (left) and animal sources (right)
Which foods in your food diary were body-building foods? Did every day of the week contain at least one?

Mushrooms belong to the fungi, not the plants. They obtain nutrients from organic matter rather than making sugars by photosynthesis. Fresh edible mushrooms contain water, fibre and nutrients, but are not interchangeable with pulses as a protein source. Never taste a wild mushroom to identify it.
3.3 The Components We Need in Tiny Amounts

Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are the components we eat by the spoonful. There is another set that we need in amounts so small they are measured in milligrams — and yet a person who goes without them falls seriously ill.
The strongest way to see what these components do is to look at what happens when they are missing. Read the two cases below and work out the answer yourself before reading on.
Case 1 — The sailors' disease

On long sea voyages in earlier centuries, sailors fell ill in a particular way. Their gums swelled and bled, their teeth loosened, old wounds reopened, and many died — often months from any battle or storm.
In May 1747, James Lind compared six treatments among twelve sailors with scurvy, two sailors per treatment. The pair receiving oranges and lemons improved most rapidly.
The condition is called scurvy.

Now interpret Case 1. Lind's sailors were not short of food — ships carried salted meat and dry biscuit in quantity. They were short of something present in lemons and oranges and absent from salted meat.

That something is now called Vitamin C. Scurvy is caused by a lack of Vitamin C in the diet, and it is prevented and cured by foods that contain it — citrus fruits like lemon and orange, and also amla, guava and green chilli.

The comparison supplied evidence favouring citrus fruit over the other treatments tested. It did not identify Vitamin C, and two sailors per treatment is a small sample. More observations and later research were needed to establish the cause.
Lind's sailors ate plenty of food and still fell ill. What does that tell you about the difference between eating enough and eating well?
Case 2 — The swelling in the neck

In the 1960s, Indian scientists studying the Himalayan region and the northern plains found that a large number of people there had a visible swelling at the front of the neck. It was common in some districts and rare in others only a few hundred kilometres away.
Following the scientists' findings, the Government of India promoted the addition of iodine to common salt — iodised salt. Where people switched to it, the swellings became far less common.
The condition is called goitre.

Iodine deficiency can enlarge the thyroid gland, causing goitre. Diets relying on crops from iodine-poor soil can contribute. But a neck swelling can have other causes: symptoms alone do not diagnose a nutrient deficiency.

Iodised salt is a way to supply a small, controlled amount of iodine through a widely used ingredient. This does not mean eating extra salt; it means using iodised salt within the usual limited amount.
You have probably read the words "iodised salt" on a packet without thinking about them. They mean common salt to which a small measured quantity of iodine salts has been added.
Vitamin C and iodine are examples of a larger group: the vitamins and minerals.

In the Little Rann of Kutch, Agariya salt workers pump underground brine into evaporation pans. Water evaporates and salt crystallises. This example connects a food ingredient to separation by evaporation and to the people who produce it.

Vitamin C and iodine are two of many. Each vitamin and each mineral has its own job, its own food sources, and its own set of symptoms when the body runs short. Together they are what keep the body's defences and daily processes working.
Fig. 3.5 sets out the main ones. Read it carefully — you will be using it again in the exercises at the end of the chapter.

Consider fictional cases. A reports bleeding gums and eats few fruits or vegetables. B reports the same symptom but eats a varied diet. Give one nutritional explanation for A. Does B rule out every nutritional cause? What information would a clinician need? Explain why a symptom and a food diary cannot establish a diagnosis.

(c) Vitamin C (d) Vitamin D

A **nutrient** is a substance the body needs for energy, growth, repair or normal functioning. Carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins and minerals are nutrient groups; water is an essential nutrient too.

The labels energy-giving, body-building and protective highlight important functions, but the jobs overlap. Proteins can supply energy, fats form parts of cells, and vitamins and minerals support many processes.
Vitamins and minerals help body processes work normally. Calling them protective does not mean that eating one food prevents every disease or treats every symptom.

This is why you are told to drink milk, eat green vegetables, eat fruit, and eat whole grains rather than only polished ones — not because these foods are filling, but because they carry the nutrients that nothing else will supply.
Vitamin D is on the list, but one of its sources is not a food at all. Which one — and what does that tell you about spending time outdoors?
3.4 Cooking, Roughage and Water
Have you noticed that a raw carrot snaps and a boiled one bends? That spinach loses its bright green in the pan?

Heat changes food, and not only in ways we can see. Some nutrients — Vitamin C among them — are partly destroyed by high heat. Washing vegetables and fruit after cutting or peeling them washes some vitamins away as well.

Two sensible conclusions follow. First, include some fruit and raw vegetables in your diet so that not everything you eat has been through a hot pan. Second, wash produce before you cut it, not after.
But do wash it. Thoroughly, every time. The vitamins lost to washing are a small price against the dirt, pesticide residue and germs that washing removes.
Two further components to consider are dietary fibre and water. Water is an essential nutrient even though it supplies no energy.

Dietary fibre, or roughage, comes mainly from plant foods such as whole grains, pulses, fruit and vegetables. Our own digestive enzymes do not break it down, although gut microbes can break down some fibre. Fibre helps bowel function; constipation can have several causes.

Water dissolves and transports substances, helps remove waste in urine and helps regulate temperature through sweating and evaporation. Needs vary with activity and weather. Water is a nutrient, not a source of food energy.
Which foods give you water besides water itself? List four.
Coluthur Gopalan (1918-2019)

To study diets in India, researchers needed reliable measurements of the foods people ate, along with records of amounts and preparation. A foreign food table could not represent every local ingredient or recipe.

Coluthur Gopalan set out to find out. Over his career he and his colleagues analysed the nutritional content of more than five hundred Indian foods — not foods from foreign tables, but the grains, pulses, vegetables and greens that Indian households actually cooked. It is difficult, unglamorous laboratory work, and it produced something India had never had: reliable numbers for its own diet.

He then led large surveys of what Indians were eating and how healthy they were. The surveys found widespread shortages of protein and energy, particularly among children — not in a few unlucky families, but across whole populations.

The national school nutrition programme began in 1995 and developed into the cooked school-meal programme now called PM POSHAN. Nutrition research helped shape school feeding policy. A programme date alone does not prove its effects: those require measurements of children and meals.
Gopalan died in 2019, aged 101.

In your notebook, compare two possible lunches using the food groups in this chapter. State what information about portion size and ingredients you would need before comparing nutrient amounts or cost.
3.5 How Do We Test for Nutrients?

So far you have taken this chapter's word for it. Time to check for yourself. Some nutrients need a well-equipped laboratory to detect. Three do not: starch, fat and protein can each be tested with equipment a school already has. Starch, incidentally, is a carbohydrate — the form in which plants store it.

Before each test, record what you expect and why. This is a prediction. Keep it beside the observation even if they disagree. Both matching and unexpected results matter; neither alone proves a complete explanation.
Activity 3.5 — Test for starch
Compare each sample with both controls. What changed? Did the controls behave as expected? What would you repeat before concluding absence?
Iodine forms a blue-black complex with starch. Compare with the starch control: a matching change supports starch being present. A negative result cannot establish absence if the control failed.
Fig. 3.7 — Testing food samples for starch
Activity 3.6 — Test for fat
Compare each sample with both controls. What changed? Did the controls behave as expected? What would you repeat before concluding absence?

Oil leaves paper translucent after water has evaporated. A persistent patch matching the oil control supports fat being present. A faint or absent patch can also depend on sample amount and transfer to the paper.
An oily patch remains translucent after the paper dries.

Make your observation table in your notebook. For each food, record your prediction, the colour before and after the starch and protein tests, and the paper-patch result for fat. Finish with three conclusions: starch present, fat present, protein present. Test potato, cucumber, boiled rice, boiled gram, peanut, bread or chapati, butter, coconut and one other food.
Activity 3.7 — Test for protein
Compare each sample with both controls. What changed? Did the controls behave as expected? What would you repeat before concluding absence?

In alkaline solution, copper ions form a violet complex with peptide bonds in proteins. Compare with the positive control before interpreting the food sample. A negative result has limits, including concentration and reagent performance.
Fig. 3.8 · Testing food samples for protein

Read across each row. Which samples gave positive results in more than one test? A food may contain several nutrients. A negative result can mean too little to detect, a preparation problem or a failed reagent: compare with your controls before concluding absence.
3.6 What Is a Balanced Diet?

Does everyone need the same food in the same amounts? Clearly not. A twelve-year-old is still growing and needs more protein for her size than her grandfather does. A farmhand doing heavy work all day needs more energy than someone at a desk. A person recovering from illness has different needs again. Requirements shift with age, sex, level of physical activity, state of health and way of life. A balanced diet is one that supplies all the nutrients a particular person needs, in the right amounts, together with enough roughage and water. Note the phrase a particular person. There is no single balanced diet for everybody — the idea only means anything once you say who is eating.
Activity 3.8 — Audit your own week
3.7 Reading the Packet
Two snacks, both sold in a packet. Compare what is printed on them.
Table 3.4 — Nutritional information per 100 g

For these example labels, chana has more protein and fibre and less fat per 100 g. That supports a comparison on those measures, not a universal ranking of foods. Portion size, ingredients and the rest of the diet also matter. Foods high in free sugars, salt or unhealthy fats can displace needed nutrients when eaten frequently.
Find a real snack packet at home. Copy its nutrition panel into your notebook. Which column of Table 3.4 does it resemble?
3.8 Millets: The Grains That Came Back

Jowar, bajra, ragi, sanwa, kodo, kutki — these are millets, and they are among the oldest cultivated grains in India. For centuries they were ordinary food across large parts of the country. Then, within a few decades, they largely disappeared from urban plates, pushed aside by polished rice and refined wheat.
Fig. 3.9 · Sanwa (barnyard millet) growing in a field
Compare the grains by named nutrients and growing conditions. A single label such as healthy cannot replace those comparisons.

Millets are small-grained cereals, so they supply carbohydrate like any cereal. What sets them apart is what comes with the carbohydrate: substantially more dietary fibre than polished rice, along with iron, calcium and B vitamins. Because of this they are often called nutri-cereals — cereals that carry protective nutrients alongside energy.

Many millets tolerate relatively dry conditions and can need less irrigation than flooded rice. Water use still depends on crop, yield, climate and farming practice. Compare like growing conditions before making a numerical claim.
Millets can add variety and nutrients and can suit dry regions. This does not make every millet superior to every rice dish on every measure.
Would millets alone be enough?

No — and the reason is worth understanding. Millets are strong on carbohydrate, fibre and several minerals, but weak on some nutrients the body needs, and no cereal supplies everything. Eaten with dal, vegetables, milk or curd, millets make an excellent meal. Eaten alone, they leave gaps.
3.9 Food Miles: From the Field to the Plate

Aarav's lunch had rice in it. Ira's had wheat. Neither grew in the school. Follow a chapati backwards from the plate and you find a chain of work. A farmer prepares soil, sows wheat, waters and tends it for months, and harvests it. The grain is threshed and winnowed to separate it from the chaff. It is stored, often for months. It is transported to a mill and ground into flour. The flour is packed, transported again, and sold in a shop. Someone buys it, carries it home, kneads it, and cooks the chapati.
That is many months, many hands, and a great many kilometres, for one item on one plate.
Fig. 3.10 · The story of a chapati: from field to plate

Food miles is the distance food travels from producer to consumer. A shorter journey may reduce transport, but total cost, freshness and emissions also depend on farming, storage, transport method and waste. Distance alone cannot establish the best choice.
3.10 Food We Throw Away
Now put the two ideas together.
Everything on your plate carries months of a farmer's work and a long journey behind it. Food left uneaten on the plate throws all of that away — the water, the labour, the fuel, the months.
The remedy is not complicated and needs no equipment. Take what you will eat. Go back for more if you are still hungry. Finish what you have taken.
How would buying food grown near your town reduce its food miles? Trace the chain in Fig. 3.10 and mark which stages would get shorter.

Recap — the chapter in short

People across India eat widely different food, and the difference is not random. It follows the crops that grow in each region, which follow soil and climate, and is then shaped by culture, religion and taste.

Culinary practices have changed sharply within living memory — from chulha to gas stove, from sil-batta to mixer-grinder — driven by new technology, better transport and faster communication. The changes brought real gains and some real losses.
• Carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins and minerals are nutrient groups studied here. Water is also an essential nutrient. Food supplies dietary fibre as well.
• Carbohydrates and fats supply energy and are called energy-giving foods. Fat carries more energy per gram than carbohydrate and is the body's store.
• Proteins build and repair the body and are called body-building foods. Growing children and athletes need proportionally more.

• Lack of a nutrient can cause a deficiency disorder. Symptoms can also have other causes, so medical assessment matters. Examples include Vitamin C deficiency causing scurvy and iodine deficiency contributing to goitre.
• Dietary fibre resists digestion by our own enzymes; gut microbes can break down some of it. Fibre helps bowel function. Water transports dissolved substances and helps regulate body temperature.

• Starch, fat and protein can be detected with simple tests: iodine turns starch blue-black, fat leaves a translucent oily patch on paper, and copper sulfate with caustic soda turns protein violet. Most foods contain more than one nutrient.
A balanced diet supplies all the nutrients a particular person needs, in the right amounts, with enough roughage and water. What is balanced depends on age, sex, activity, health and way of life.

• Junk foods carry plenty of energy from sugar and fat and little else. Millets are called nutri-cereals because they carry fibre and minerals along with their carbohydrate, and they grow on less water.
• Food miles measures distance, not total environmental impact. Transport method, farming and storage also matter. Wasted food wastes resources used to produce it.

Practice — Apply

7. Ira records few vegetables, fruits or whole grains in her diary and has difficulty passing stool. Which food component might be low? Suggest sources and state why the diary cannot establish the medical cause of her symptoms.

8. Reshma has trouble seeing in dim light. Her doctor prescribes a vitamin supplement and advises a change of diet. (i) Which deficiency disorder does she most likely have? (ii) Which nutrient is short in her diet? (iii) Name four foods she should include.

9. Gourav fractures his leg. His doctor sets the bone, applies a plaster, and prescribes calcium tablets. At the next visit the doctor adds Vitamin D syrup. Use Fig. 3.5 to answer: (i) Why calcium? (ii) Why add Vitamin D alongside it, rather than more calcium? (iii) What question would you want to ask the doctor?
10. You are offered canned fruit juice, freshly squeezed juice, and a whole fresh fruit. Which would you choose, and why? Give two reasons, at least one of them about a nutrient.
11. Sugar is a carbohydrate, but sugar tested with iodine does not turn blue-black. What does this tell you about the relationship between sugar and starch?

12. A drop of iodine solution falls on Ira's cotton socks and another on her teacher's silk saree. The drop on the saree turns blue-black; the drop on the socks does not. Suggest an explanation. (Think about what is used to stiffen cloth.)

13. Explain how iodine-poor soil could contribute to iodine deficiency in a local diet. How does iodised salt help prevent it? Why should a person with neck swelling seek medical assessment rather than diagnose themselves?

14. Two snacks weigh the same. One lists 8 g protein and 3 g fibre per 100 g; the other lists 3 g protein and 1 g fibre, with twice the fat. Which is the better everyday snack? Justify your answer using the numbers.
Practice — Reason and Investigate

15. Raman says: "All starches are carbohydrates, but not all carbohydrates are starches." Is he right? Design an activity that would test his claim, stating what you would use, what you would do, and what result would support him.

16. A teacher provides known iodine solution, starch paste and water. Design positive and negative controls for a starch test. What would a failed positive control mean for a negative food result? Never test or taste an unlabelled chemical.

17. Millets grow on less water and carry more fibre and minerals than polished rice. Yet polished rice replaced millets across much of urban India. Suggest two reasons why a food that is worse on nutrition might still win. (Consider cost, cooking time, storage, and what people believe about food.)

18. Lind compared six treatments in 1747, with two sailors per treatment. What does this comparison support? What does it not establish? Explain how a larger, repeated comparison would strengthen the evidence.
Beyond the Book

• Read three labels. Next time groceries are unpacked at home, find three packaged items and copy their nutrition panels. Rank them from best to worst as an everyday food and write two lines defending your ranking.

Salt without a factory. The Apatani people of Arunachal Pradesh traditionally make a salt called tapyo from plant ash rather than from seawater or rock. Find out how, and why a community would develop such a method. Write a short account with pictures.

Wild food near you. In many parts of India people gather uncultivated greens, fruit and mushrooms — the ranbhajis of Maharashtra are one example. find out whether anything is gathered wild near your town. Ask an older person; they will know things the internet does not.

• Write to your principal. With your classmates, list the junk foods most often eaten in your school. Then write a joint letter to your principal proposing which to remove from the canteen and what to offer instead. Cost your alternatives — a proposal nobody can afford will be refused.
